### Company description and business model

Diversified Healthcare Trust is a Maryland healthcare REIT that earns income in two ways. Managed senior living communities are leased to its own taxable subsidiaries and run by third-party managers for a fee, and medical office and life science properties are let to tenants under net, modified gross and full-service leases; a small book of triple net leased senior living and wellness properties adds contractual rent. Revenue in the larger segment is residents' fees that move with occupancy and rate, so cash flow visibility is lower than for a net lease REIT and operating leverage is high. The portfolio changed in 2025, when 69 properties were sold and the medical office base shrank; senior housing now produces 87.01% of revenue and 61.5% of net operating income, which ties debt service to operator performance in one segment.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 10–11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 30; calculation M7
### Ownership and group structure

The trust is a public REIT with no sponsor fund and no equity cure behind it. ABP Trust and the chair hold 9.8% of the shares and control the parent of the external manager, which employs every officer and holds agreements to 2045 with a termination fee of 19 years to 20 years of fees, so governance leverage for creditors rests on independent Trustees. Debt sits at the parent and at property-owning subsidiaries: the 4.375% notes due 2031 carry unsecured subsidiary guarantees, the 7.25% notes due 2030 are secured on the equity of subsidiaries owning 36 properties, and the other three unsecured series carry no guarantee, so they rank behind USD 841.40 million of secured principal and behind the creditors of subsidiaries. Financial policy has been conservative in conduct: small distributions, no acquisitions in 2023, 2024 or 2025, and property sales applied to debt; detailed ranking and legal capacity belong to Structural priority and Legal & covenants, for which the debt documents are not supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 13–15, 26, 50–51; 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 124–125, 195, 213
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Residents' fees are 91.11% basic housing and support services paid privately and 6.40% from Medicare and Medicaid, so volume and rate drive revenue and government reimbursement is a small exposure. Occupancy across all senior housing properties was 83.8% in Q3 2026 against 81.5% a year earlier and the average monthly rate was USD 5,670 against USD 5,472, a rise of 3.62%, so rate has carried part of the gain. The trust cites constrained supply, with inventory growth of 0.5% and absorption of 2.8% in the fourth quarter of 2025 from a third-party source, which supports occupancy but is a management reading. Medical office and life science revenue is contractual but shrinking, at USD 40.40 million against USD 48.20 million in Q3, with 20.3% of annualized rental income expiring in 2028 and a weighted average remaining term of 4.9 years; new and renewal leases in Q3 2026 were signed at a rental rate change of 25.2%. Revenue is recurring in form, cyclical in occupancy and concentrated in one segment, and the filings describe no long-term contract protection for resident revenue.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 31–33; 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8; calculation M11
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Costs follow the operation of the communities and sit with the managers: labor and benefits were 48.18% of segment revenue in Q3 2026 against 51.72% a year earlier and management fees 5.68% against 5.31%, with insurance, utilities and food the other named pressures. Net operating income margin rose to 15.52% from 8.88% and part of that gain reflects a smaller portfolio, since units fell from 24,906 to 22,445, so the margin is both an improvement and a base for operating deleverage. Management fees move with revenue and incentive fees share the upside above target EBITDA, so lenders bear the downside. The issuer expects labor, insurance and food cost increases to moderate, which is a management view; margins can be defended under modest volume pressure but not under a combined wage and occupancy shock.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11, 20, 30–31; 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation M4; calculation M12
### Capital intensity and free cash flow conversion

Capital intensity is high against cash earnings. Real estate improvements were USD 118.66 million over the last twelve months against operating cash flow of USD 54.01 million, so free cash flow after interest was negative at USD 64.65 million, and EBITDA does not convert to free cash flow available for debt reduction. Recurring capital expenditure, the issuer's non-GAAP figure, was USD 67.80 million for nine months 2026 against USD 96.38 million, and the issuer guides USD 90.00 million to USD 105.00 million for 2026; the trust says it may defer certain redevelopment projects to preserve liquidity, which is a lever, and cash taxes are small at USD 3.18 million for nine months. Cash interest of USD 193.02 million over the last twelve months includes USD 65.88 million of accreted interest paid in the fourth quarter of 2025, which will not recur.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 8, 47–48; EX99.1_2026-09-30_dhc_tm2629915d1-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 22; calculation M1
### Porter's Five Forces

Competitive rivalry matters through occupancy: senior housing competes community by community, and supply growth is low at 0.5% a year in the trust's cited data, which limits the pressure on occupancy and rate. The threat of new entrants is restrained by the cost of financing and construction, which the annual report names as the reason supply has stayed low, so competitors cannot quickly add units and dilute pricing. Buyer power is moderate: residents pay mostly privately and monthly rates rose 3.62% in a year, while medical office tenants renewed at higher rents, so there is no evidence of pricing pressure; the threat of substitutes, such as home care, is not established in the sources. Supplier power is the weaker side: labor is the largest cost line at 48.18% of segment revenue and the trust relies on managers that set rents and hire staff, so wage inflation and manager performance are the forces that most affect margin and cash flow.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8, 11–12, 88; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 30–32; calculation M11; calculation M12
### PEST

PEST factors are only partly a primary credit driver. Regulatory exposure is small, because Medicare and Medicaid are 6.40% of residents' fees and only a small amount of net operating income comes from properties that depend mainly on them; economic factors matter more, through labor inflation, interest rates and the financing market that sets the cost of refinancing the 2028 maturities; the social factor, a growing population aged 75 and over at about 4% a year between 2025 and 2035 on the trust's cited census projection, supports demand; technological factors do not appear to be a primary credit driver in the materials provided.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 30, 52
### SWOT

Strengths: senior housing net operating income up 67.66% in a year; no scheduled principal of note before 2028; 94.27% of principal at fixed rates; asset sales that reduced debt without distributions; rating upgrades. Weaknesses: net leverage of about 8x to 9x; cash interest cover of 1.34x; negative free cash flow; concentration in one segment and in a few managers; governance that depends on an externally managed structure. Opportunities that could improve credit quality: further occupancy and margin gains toward the market levels the issuer cites, sale proceeds applied to debt, and refinancing of the 2028 maturities early. Threats that could weaken it: wage and insurance inflation, operator transitions on six communities and on the Ensign lease, manager failure, revolver access limited by covenants, and refinancing at a higher coupon.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11, 30, 52; calculation M1; calculation M4
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are average: gross real estate book value is USD 6,274.29 million across the portfolio, large enough to absorb disposals, but no market share data is supplied. Competitive advantage is not assessable: no peer or market data is supplied and operations are outsourced. Business diversification is average: five managers hold 77.4% of gross real estate book value and the segment is 61.5% of net operating income, but the properties sit in 33 states. Cost and capex flexibility is average: capital spending can be deferred, but labor is 48.18% of segment revenue. Margin stability is weak: segment margin rose from 8.88% to 15.52% in a year, which shows how far it can swing. Free cash flow stability is weak: free cash flow was negative at USD 89.48 million for 2024, USD 166.44 million for 2025 and USD 64.65 million trailing. Ability to refinance is average and improving: the 2025 refinancing worked and ratings rose, but USD 640.61 million falls due in 2028. Liquidity position is average: USD 260.66 million covers near-term maturities many times but only 0.41x of 2028, and covenant headroom is not established. Financial policy and governance is average: behaviour is benign, but control sits with the external manager. The main supports are the earnings recovery, the maturity profile to 2028 and conservative financial policy; the main constraints are leverage, thin cover and negative free cash flow; the trend is improving; the missing datapoints are covenant levels, peer data and the proxy statement.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 20, 30–31; calculation M1; calculation M3; calculation M13
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next twelve to twenty-four months the issuer guides 2026 Adjusted EBITDAre of USD 275.70 million to USD 290.70 million and interest expense of USD 149.00 million, which would give cover of about 1.90x on guidance, a management view not reconciled to GAAP. Tailwinds are senior housing occupancy and rate momentum, constrained supply, a lease with Ensign that converts seven skilled nursing facilities to contractual rent from 2026-10-01, and fixed-rate debt. Headwinds are labor and insurance costs, the January 2027 incentive fee of USD 29.30 million if earned, operator transitions, the expiry of the interest rate cap in March 2027 before the loan's March 2028 maturity, and a 2028 maturity wall that comes inside twelve months from February 2027. Over three to five years the question is whether earnings growth and asset sales bring leverage toward the issuer's stated target of 5.5x to 6.5x excluding incentive fees, which would require debt reduction: at the third-quarter run rate excluding incentive fees net leverage would be 7.28x, and reaching the top of the range would take about USD 244.75 million of net debt reduction.
Basis: EX99.1_2026-09-30_dhc_tm2629915d1-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 6, 8; 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 11, 15, 23, 34; calculation M10
### Qualitative downside scenario

The initiating condition is a reversal in senior housing during 2027: occupancy, now 83.8%, stalls or labor and insurance costs jump, or a large manager underperforms, the largest holding communities worth 30.5% of gross book value. The first operational break is segment margin, now 15.52%; each percentage point on annualised segment revenue is about USD 12.80 million of earnings, or 4.58% of trailing Adjusted EBITDAre. Financial transmission is immediate because interest is 94.27% fixed: earnings fall against unchanged interest, cover of 1.34x on cash interest tightens, free cash flow, already negative at USD 64.65 million trailing, widens, and net leverage rises from 8.20x on the adjusted measure. Even a fall back to the 2025 level of USD 266.08 million would leave net leverage at 8.62x with no debt reduction. The liquidity effect is that cash of USD 110.66 million funds the deficit and the January 2027 incentive fee, while the USD 150.00 million revolver depends on covenants that are not supplied. The refinancing effect arrives as the 2028 maturities enter their last twelve months from February 2027: replacing the notes due February 2028 at a 7.25% coupon adds USD 12.50 million a year. Management levers are deferring redevelopment, selling properties as it did in 2025 and 2026 and a distribution of only USD 9.66 million a year; they appear sufficient to avoid liquidity distress through 2027 because scheduled principal before 2028 is USD 2.55 million, but not sufficient to refinance 2028 without market access. The observable triggers are quarterly occupancy and margin, manager terminations, revolver statements and any refinancing announcement.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11, 16, 30–31, 54; calculation M3; calculation M4; calculation M5; calculation M9
### Primary downside path

Primary downside path: a margin reversal in the managed senior housing portfolio against fixed interest and negative free cash flow, which pushes the 2028 maturities into a refinancing that liquidity cannot cover.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation M3; calculation M4
### Overall credit view

Overall, Diversified Healthcare Trust presents an adequate but concentrated business profile supported by an improving senior housing portfolio, a maturity profile with little principal before 2028 and benign financial policy, but credit quality is constrained by leverage of about 8x to 9x, thin cover and negative free cash flow. Cash-flow durability appears weak because capital spending exceeds operating cash flow. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on continued margin gains, asset sales and the covenant terms of the revolver. The primary downside path is a margin reversal ahead of the 2028 maturities. Further analysis would require the credit agreement and indentures, covenant levels, peer and market data and the proxy statement. The fundamental credit synthesis is complete. Top risk: the 2028 refinancing against negative free cash flow.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation M1; calculation M3

## Gaps

- Covenant levels, definitions, step-downs and headroom are not supplied, so the usability of the undrawn USD 150,000 thousand revolver and every liquidity conclusion rests on the issuer's statement that it believed it complied at 2026-09-30. Severity: High. Action: obtain the credit agreement, indentures and compliance certificates.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 16, 49–50; Source readiness (CP-0)

- The debt documents are not supplied, so legal capacity for restricted payments, further secured debt and guarantee releases, and the ranking among the separately secured debts, are not established; Structural priority and Legal & covenants cannot be completed. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the executed documents.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 13–16, 60–62; Source readiness (CP-0)

- The value of unencumbered assets is not established: the November 2026 presentation shows two figures, USD 4.0 billion and USD 4.2 billion, and the quarterly report prints no total, so the capacity to raise secured debt to meet the 2028 maturities cannot be measured. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the issuer's schedule of unencumbered properties.
Basis: EX99.1_2026-09-30_dhc_tm2629915d1-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, page 8; Source readiness (CP-0)

- No peer filings, market quotes or agency reports are supplied, so the business profile cannot be set against comparable issuers and the cost of refinancing is illustrated from the coupon of the 2025 secured notes. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain peer and pricing data.
Basis: Source readiness (CP-0)

- EBITDA is derived and the adjusted measure is the issuer's, with a definition change in the third quarter of 2026; the net debt and interest inputs behind the issuer's stated 8.2x and 2.0x are not printed. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the quarterly financial supplements.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); EX99.1_2026-09-30_dhc_tm2629915d1-ex99-1-htm.htm.jsonl, pages 8, 20–21

- The proxy statement is not supplied, so board committee structure, independence determinations and the share ownership table are not established. Severity: Low. Action: obtain the 2026 proxy statement.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

- The performance of individual managers and communities, and any seasonality in senior housing earnings, are not disclosed, so the earnings recovery cannot be attributed to particular operators and the third-quarter dip from the second quarter cannot be read as trend or season. Severity: Low. Action: compare like quarters in later reports.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11, 31

- Substitutes for senior living, such as home care, and market share are not covered in the sources, so competitive position is described only through occupancy, rate and supply statistics the trust cites. Severity: Low. Action: obtain independent sector data.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_dhc.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8
